rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Apple just named their smart home hub, priced it, and put it on sale — today.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: HomeView. Two hundred and ninety-nine dollars. Ships November thirteenth.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And it watches your face to decide what to show you. Which is either convenient or the plot of a short film.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: We've got that, Meta's new agents that are built to actually finish your work, and a major AI startup that just filed for bankruptcy and sold pieces of itself to Disney. Stay with us.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. When AI news moves this fast, knowing what happened is not enough; you need to know what changes your next decision. The Ledger turns the day’s noise into five focused briefings for people who need the consequence before consensus catches up. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So Apple's HomeView. What actually is this thing?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's a display with a speaker, sits in your kitchen or your hallway, runs an updated version of Siri, and controls your smart home devices. Think of it like a smart screen you'd talk to — but Apple's version.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Like an Amazon Echo Show, but in a turtleneck.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Essentially. Except the thing Apple is really pushing is that it knows who you are.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Walk me through that.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The device has cameras and it uses them to recognize individual people in the household. So when you walk up, it shows your calendar, your messages, your apps. When your partner walks up, it shows theirs. It changes the whole experience based on who's standing in front of it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is the bit that requires you to trust Apple with a fairly permanent record of everyone who lives in your home.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. Is that creepy or just convenient?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I think the honest answer is it's both, depending entirely on how much you already trust Apple with your data.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And three hundred dollars.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's a real number. How does that sit against the competition?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Amazon's Echo Show comes in well under that. Google's Nest Hub is cheaper too. Apple is charging a premium and betting that the personalization plus the ecosystem lock-in justifies it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which it might, if you're already deep in the Apple world. If your phone is an iPhone, your laptop is a Mac, your watch is an Apple Watch — this device probably slots in pretty smoothly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And if you're not?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Then you've bought a three hundred dollar screen that would very much prefer you were.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What about third-party smart home devices? Can it actually control things from other brands?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Apple hasn't fully established that in the announcement materials. The source material we have is clear on the Apple ecosystem and Siri integration. Third-party compatibility and regional availability aren't confirmed yet.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So you might buy this thing and discover your existing smart lights or thermostat from a different brand just doesn't cooperate.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That is a genuine open question. And it's not a trivial one.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's worth flagging though — the personalization feature, the face-recognition piece — that's actually the part I find interesting rather than alarming. Every other smart display in your home treats the whole household as one user. This one tries to distinguish between you and your kids and whoever else lives there.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Give me a use case.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Say hypothetically you walk into the kitchen at seven in the morning and the thing shows you your nine AM meeting, your grocery reminder, and a message from your sister. Your teenager walks up at seven thirty and it shows them their school schedule and the texts their friends sent overnight. Same device —

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: completely different experience.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's actually useful.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It is. The question is whether Siri is capable enough to make that experience feel seamless rather than janky.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's a fair concern. Siri has had a complicated decade.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Apple says it's an updated Siri. What that means in practice — how much better, at what tasks — that's the part we don't know until people actually have the device in hand.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing I'm still turning over — Apple says the device shows you person-specific notes, contacts, calendar appointments. That's not just your calendar. That's everything.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. And it's all sitting on a display in a shared room. So if someone walks into your kitchen while you're not there, do they see your messages?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's actually the design question that matters more than the price.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Because the personalization only works if the device knows nobody else is looking.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And we don't know how it handles that. Does it blank the screen when you step away? Does it require you to walk up before it shows anything sensitive?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Apple hasn't specified that in what's been released. Which is a notable gap for a device built around the idea that your household data is private to you.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: It could be that this is the thing that makes or breaks the product in actual use. Not the face recognition itself — but what the device does with your information when you're not the one standing there.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Alex, for what it's worth, this would solve exactly none of your smart home problems.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: My smart home is fine.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Your kitchen light has been stuck on a Tuesday schedule since March.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And yet — three hundred dollars might fix it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: It absolutely would not fix it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: No. But the November reviews will at least tell us what it does fix.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One more thing I want to flag — FaceTime is a confirmed feature on this. That's not nothing on a kitchen device.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the one that makes most sense to me in a shared room. Video calls on a screen that's already in the place where your family gathers.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It also makes it the most expensive speakerphone you've ever purchased.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Three hundred dollars to call your mum from the kitchen.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: She'll be delighted. The device, arguably less so. November thirteenth. We'll find out what the screen does when nobody's standing there.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the honest summary is: hardware sounds capable, personalization concept is genuinely new, but ecosystem lock-in is real and third-party compatibility is unconfirmed.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And three hundred dollars is a commitment before those questions have answers.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Preorders open today. Which means Apple is asking you to decide before any independent reviews exist.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's how Apple always does it, to be fair.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: If you're all-in on Apple already and you've been meaning to sort your smart home out — this is probably the most interesting thing in this category right now. If you're not, wait for the reviews in November.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Or buy the cheaper one and spend the difference on something that makes you happy.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus, the people's economist.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our second story. Meta launched two new AI models yesterday — Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full. And the reason this matters isn't just "new model." It's what these models are actually built to do. Jamie, what's the core idea?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So most AI models you've used are conversational. You ask something, they answer. You ask again, they answer. Each exchange is basically its own thing. What Meta is pitching here is different — these models are built for what's called agentic workflows. Which just means: give the AI a multi-step task, walk away — and it handles it without you babysitting every step.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Like a to-do list that does itself.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: If the to-do list involved planning, using software tools, hitting a snag, working around the snag, and finishing the job — yes, exactly like that.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And they've added something called Active Memory. Yesterday we had an open question about whether the new Meta models would support persistent memory across sessions or just within a single conversation. Does this answer it?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It does. Active Memory is confirmed in the source — it retains context across sessions, not just within one. So if you're running a project over several days, the model remembers where you left off.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which sounds like a small thing and is actually significant. The failure mode for most agents right now is that they're goldfish. Every session, you're starting from scratch.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And there's Active Focus — what does that one do?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Active Focus is about task blockers. When an automated task hits a problem — a missing piece of information, a step that doesn't work as expected — most models just stop and wait for a human. Active Focus is designed to work through those blockers on its own.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So it doesn't just get stuck.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the claim. The important qualification is that the benchmarks cited are from Meta's own internal testing. Independent evaluation hasn't happened yet.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So "doesn't just get stuck" is what Meta says. How often it actually doesn't get stuck is an entirely separate question.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Fair. Rufus, take us on location.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Right. Picture a midsize software company in New York — a developer team that's been running Claude or GPT for their automation pipeline. They open their laptops this morning and they have a new option to price out.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Muse Code Power is fifty dollars a month. Maximum is two hundred a month. Those are the tiers that unlock Muse Wonder Full.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is the classic enterprise land-and-expand structure. Get developers comfortable on the accessible, cheaper model through the API, and then when they need the more capable version for production workloads, the only path forward is a subscription tier.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Or you could read it as: they built a genuinely more capable model and they're pricing it for the enterprise customers who can actually afford it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Both can be true simultaneously.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's exactly what bothers me about it. Without independent benchmarks, we can't tell whether Muse Wonder Full is actually worth the subscription, or whether the performance gap between Wonder and Wonder Full is real or essentially manufactured.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A valid concern. Meta says the benchmarks support the capability gap. We're waiting for someone outside Meta to confirm that.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing I keep wanting to pin down — Active Memory retains context across sessions. But how long are we actually talking? A project that runs a few days, or something that spans weeks?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The source says across sessions. It doesn't specify a limit. Which is either genuinely open-ended, or a detail Meta hasn't published yet.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A one-million-token context window is enormous either way. That's roughly the length of several novels worth of conversation history the model can hold at once.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the memory problem might be less about capacity and more about whether the model uses that context usefully over time.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which brings us back to Active Focus. Because remembering where you left off only matters if the model can actually continue from there without making different mistakes on day four than it made on day one.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And that is precisely what Meta's internal benchmarks claim it does. Which is precisely what we cannot verify.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Here's what I'd want to know before spending two hundred dollars a month — does Active Focus actually reduce how often a human has to step back in, or does it just delay the moment you have to?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's not a question Meta's announcement answers. That's a question for the developers who run it against real workloads.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Both models also support planning and tool use natively. So the agent can call external software, not just process text. That's worth noting — it's not just a smarter chat window.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which makes the independent benchmark question more urgent, not less. Back to the wider story. Yesterday on the show we asked whether developers would pay two hundred a month for an AI agent that reliably handles multi-step work tasks. The key word is reliably. That's what Active Focus is supposed to deliver.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And Rufus called the land-and-expand strategy before we even had the product details confirmed. The pricing structure is exactly what he predicted.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I have my moments.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The practical question for developers right now is whether Muse Wonder at four dollars per million tokens performs well enough for most agentic workflows, or whether you genuinely need Wonder Full. And you cannot answer that yet without independent testing.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The context window is one million tokens on both models, which is large. That part isn't gated behind the subscription.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The memory is universal. The capability ceiling is not.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the argument from yesterday — whether this is a standard enterprise pricing pattern or something closer to vendor lock-in — today's details don't close that debate.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It is, at minimum, a subscription Meta would very much like you to remain inside.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Alex, if everything is breaking news, when are we supposed to get any work done?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the question The Ledger helps you work through: five focused briefings connecting AI news with the decisions in front of you.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The Ledger. Because reading another headline is a marvellous way to postpone deciding anything. I admire the efficiency of the procrastination.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus has diagnosed the problem. The Ledger link is in our show notes. Back to the story.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our third story today, and this one lands differently. Character.AI — a company that built one of the most talked-about consumer AI platforms of the last few years — filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on October twelfth and agreed to sell some of its assets to Disney for twenty million dollars. Jamie, what happened?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Character.AI was a platform that let users create and talk to AI characters — fictional personas, celebrities, companions. It was enormously popular. Tens of millions of users. And then it ran into a combination of legal exposure, compute costs, and the basic problem of turning engagement into sustainable revenue.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Twenty million dollars from Disney. That feels low for a company that had that level of usage.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It is low. The court filing lists assets and liabilities both in the range of fifty to a hundred million dollars. The twenty million from Disney is for some assets — not all of them, not the whole company.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And there is not yet a bid for the remaining assets. The company said itself that if no bid emerges, the platform could be wound down.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So users could just wake up one day and it's gone.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's a live possibility. The company says it will keep operating during the sale process, which is expected to close in late November or early December. But "keep operating during the sale process" is not the same as a guaranteed future.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What does Disney actually get for twenty million?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Some assets, and transition services from former Character.AI employees who have since joined Disney. So it's partly technology and partly talent in a structured handover. A fairly classic IP-and-people acquisition wrapped inside a bankruptcy process.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which tells you something about what Disney valued. It wasn't necessarily the platform or the user base — it was specific technology and the people who built it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What do you think Disney does with it?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Speculation on my part, but there's an obvious application. Disney has some of the most valuable fictional characters ever created. If they acquired technology that was specifically trained to make AI characters feel engaging and persistent — that has very clear uses inside their own product ecosystem.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is interesting. And also slightly grim from the perspective of the people who used Character.AI for what it was.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which was what, exactly? Because I want to make sure we're honest about this platform.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It was a lot of things. Some people used it for creative writing. Some used it as a kind of social space. Some people formed what felt like genuine connections with characters — particularly teenagers and people who were lonely or isolated. There were lawsuits involving harms to minors. The company was under serious legal and reputational pressure.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The compute costs were also real. Running this kind of conversational AI at massive scale is expensive. The revenue model — which is to say, the way they were planning to make money — never caught up with the cost of running the thing.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Here's what I keep coming back to. This company was not obscure. Massive engagement. And it still couldn't sustain itself. The compute costs didn't care.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is the part that should interest anyone who follows this space. Engagement and revenue are not the same thing — and for Character.AI, the gap between those two numbers is what put them in court.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what's the watch here? What do we look for next?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Whether Disney's involvement becomes something users actually see — like, does this technology end up in a Disney product that keeps some version of these characters alive — or whether it's purely a behind-the-scenes IP acquisition that means nothing to the people who used the platform.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And whether any other bidder emerges for the rest of the assets. That determines whether Character.AI as a platform survives in any form or disappears entirely.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The Reuters reporting is clear that there's no bid for all assets yet. That's the thing to watch. The window closes late November, early December.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I'll just say — the people who built communities on this platform, who had years of conversations saved there — they deserve a straight answer about what happens to those conversations and whether they lose access.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That answer isn't in the filing yet.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: We'll track it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: All right. We opened with Apple HomeView. The title question: is it worth your money?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: If you're already committed to the Apple ecosystem — iPhone, Mac, the whole stack — and you want a smart home hub that actually personalizes itself for different people in your household, this is the most interesting product in that category right now. The personalization concept is real and it's new.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The honest answer is that nobody outside Apple knows yet whether Siri is good enough to make that personalization feel smooth rather than frustrating. November thirteenth is when we get actual devices in actual hands.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the specific thing to do: if you want an Apple home hub, put preorders on your radar but wait for independent reviews in the second week of November before committing three hundred dollars. Third-party compatibility is still an open question.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And if this episode was useful, share the Character.AI story. It's the thing that surprised us most today — that a platform with millions of users and real cultural presence could end up in bankruptcy court selling pieces of itself to Disney for twenty million dollars. The useful payoff — high engagement does not equal a sustainable business. That's worth knowing before you build on somebody else's platform or become dependent on one.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That applies whether you're a developer, an investor, or someone whose data lives on a service that hasn't figured out how to charge for itself.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s question for you: Would you pay $299 for a smart home hub that recognizes you and personalizes your home screen?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A quick final note: today’s episode was brought to you by The Ledger—decision-grade AI signal for people who cannot afford to be late.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What changed. Who wins. What you do next. That’s The AI Edge. Follow The AI Edge now. Join us tomorrow for what changes next.
